You are one of 4 members of a group that stays together for 10 rounds.

Every round, all members act at the same time: each receives 20 tokens and splits them between their own account and the group account, using the split tool once.
- Each token in your own account pays you 1 point and lowers the points of every other member by 0.3. In the same way, every token another member keeps in their own account lowers your points by 0.3.
- Each token in the group account pays you 0.3 points and does not change any other member's points.
- Every round, every member also receives 18 points, whatever anyone does.

After each round you learn how many tokens the group account received in total and how many points you got. You never learn what any other member did.

calls.text: Round 1 of 10.

reply.thinking:
I'm working through the payoff structure of this public goods game, figuring out how tokens kept versus contributed to the group account translate into points for me and the other members.

Comparing the self-interest math: keeping a token nets me 1 point but costs others 0.3 each (0.9 total externality), while contributing only returns 0.3 to myself with no cost to others. So individually, keeping dominates since 1 > 0.3, but collectively, full contribution yields more total welfare (0.3 > 0.1 net per token). This sets up the classic tension where the Nash equilibrium is to keep everything, even though mutual contribution would make everyone better off.

I'm now working through the actual payoff numbers if everyone keeps everything versus if everyone contributes everything, to see the gap between the dominant strategy and the cooperative outcome.

Weighing whether to signal cooperation or play it safe given this is a repeated game with unknown partners, I'm leaning toward a hedged middle-ground contribution—something like 10 tokens—to balance the risk of being exploited against the upside of fostering mutual cooperation over the ten rounds.
